blocks.html: It is a great shame and baseness (said Paul the Jurisconsult), and a patent confession of the matter in question, to be willing neither to swear nor to tender the oath a; for even where all other proofs should fail b, nay, where there should be some presumption against him who tenders it, and he were charged with the proof, it would nevertheless be lawful for him, to cut [the matter] short and search out the truth, to tender the oath to his party c: who can have no just reason for not swearing, inasmuch as from a party he is made judge, by the will and consent of his adversary d. I say this, saving what our Interpreters discourse of it more amply in the common places [the titles where the subject is ordinarily treated], and what we shall write of it a little hereafter e.

notes.citation: Digest 12.2.38 (De iureiurando sive voluntario sive necessario sive iudiciali, l. Manifestae; Paul: Manifestae turpitudinis et confessionis est nolle nec iurare nec iusiurandum referre)
notes.original: I. manife. ſta. D. de iure iuran.
notes.gloss: The print's I. is l.; the fragment is the text Coras paraphrases.

notes.citation: Code 6.30.22 (De iure deliberandi et de adeunda vel adquirenda hereditate; Justinian's law Scimus, the last of the title — the print's l. ſi. is l. Sci[mus]), § 10 (Licentia danda creditoribus seu legatariis vel fideicommissariis … vel per sacramentum illius, si aliae probationes defecerint: the heir's oath on the inventory where all other proofs fail); Digest 12.2.35 (De iureiurando, l. Tutor pupilli; Paul)
notes.original: l. ſi. P. licen tia. C. de iur. de lib. l. tutor pupilli. D. de iure iu.
notes.gloss: The title de iur. de lib. is read as de iure deliberandi; the P. stands for the paragraph sign.

notes.citation: Code 6.42.32 (De fideicommissis), the last law of the title (Justinian, Quaestionem ex facto emergentem…)
notes.gloss: The bearing of this law on the oath tendered by the party charged with the proof could not be verified.

notes.citation: The Doctors (commentators) on the law Manifestae already cited (at {a})
notes.original: Les Docteurs en la l. manifeſta al leguee.
notes.gloss: The commonplace that he to whom the oath is tendered is made judge of the cause by the consent of his adversary.

Annotation XV treats the corruption of a slave and does not discuss the oath, and Coras says the discussion is to come "a little hereafter"; the number is probably a wrong sort for a later annotation, on Bertrande's refusal to swear. Given as printed.
